title: Rescinds DOJ Phase-Out of Private Prisons
description_short: Attorney General Jeff Sessions reversed the Obama-era plan to phase out private federal prisons.
description_medium: In 2017, Attorney General Jeff Sessions rescinded the Justice Department’s plan to reduce federal reliance on private prisons, reversing an Obama-era phase-out. The decision restored the department’s ability to use private prison contracts for federal inmates. It shifted policy toward continued use of for-profit operators and renewed debate over their role in federal incarceration.
subcategory: Mass Prison Privatization and Forced Labor

title: EPA Weakens Coal Ash Disposal Rules
description_short: EPA issued a final rule amending coal ash disposal regulations, loosening requirements for coal ash facilities.
description_medium: The EPA finalized amendments that loosened coal-ash disposal requirements for power plants. Coal ash is waste from coal-fired electricity generation, and storage rules affect how facilities manage material near land and waterways. The final rule weakened federal safeguards for handling the waste at facilities and nearby communities.

preserved_fields.description_short: EPA issued a final rule amending coal ash disposal regulations, loosening requirements for coal ash facilities.

title: Chris Wright Energy Secretary Accelerates Fossil Fuels and Kills Clean Energy Programs
description_short: Chris Wright Energy Secretary Accelerates Fossil Fuels and Kills Clean Energy Programs
description_medium: Energy Secretary Chris Wright — a former fracking company CEO who had publicly denied climate change — aggressively accelerated fossil fuel production permits and approvals while terminating, reversing, or defunding clean energy programs funded by the Inflation Reduction Act. Wright used the Department of Energy to serve the interests of the oil and gas industry he had led, implementing policies that industry lobbyists had written. Climate scientists warned the energy policy reversal locked in catastrophic warming scenarios that would be impossible to reverse.
description_long: On February 5, 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed his first departmental order, directing the Department of Energy to implement President Trump’s energy agenda. The document calls for expanding domestic production and lowering costs, accelerating work at national laboratories, refilling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, modernizing the nuclear weapons stockpile, supporting commercial nuclear power, strengthening grid reliability, and streamlining permits. It also refers to weapons stewardship and Cold War waste-cleanup commitments, placing energy supply priorities alongside the department’s security and cleanup missions. The order directs DOE to remove barriers to private energy investment and prioritize more efficient permitting. It set administrative priorities around energy abundance, production, affordability, and reliability. The order established a policy direction; effects on individual grants, permits, or clean-energy programs depend on subsequent department actions. Its priorities span fuel production, nuclear technology, transmission infrastructure, and laboratory research rather than a single project or permit.

title: Steven Mnuchin Treasury Secretary — Requested Government Jet for Honeymoon, Eclipse Trip
description_short: Steven Mnuchin Treasury Secretary — Requested Government Jet for Honeymoon, Eclipse Trip
description_medium: In 2017, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin requested a government jet for his European honeymoon, citing secure-communications needs; officials later deemed the request unnecessary. That August, he used a government aircraft for a trip to Louisville and Fort Knox on the day of a solar eclipse. The Treasury inspector general reviewed whether the trip complied with travel, ethics, and appropriations rules.
description_long: In summer 2017, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin requested a government jet for a European honeymoon with his wife, Louise Linton, citing the need for secure communications. Treasury officials later concluded the aircraft was unnecessary, and the request was not carried out. A separate trip occurred on August 21, when Mnuchin flew to Louisville and Fort Knox on a government plane with Linton, the day of a total solar eclipse visible in the area. The itinerary drew questions about whether the travel was official or partly motivated by the eclipse. The Treasury inspector general opened a review of whether applicable travel, ethics, and appropriations rules were followed. The two episodes raised related but distinct questions about taxpayer-funded travel: officials rejected the personal honeymoon request, while the eclipse-day flight actually occurred and drew an inspector-general review. No aircraft was ultimately furnished for the honeymoon, but the later itinerary used a government plane.

title: Trump's constitutional dictatorship
description_medium: In a 2026 New York Review of Books essay on Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s book, Mark Danner argued that Trump expanded executive power by invoking emergencies and using executive orders. Danner also criticized congressional Republicans for allowing those assertions to go unchecked. “Constitutional dictatorship” is the essay’s political characterization, not a court finding.
description_long: Mark Danner’s 2026 review of Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s book argues that Trump used emergency powers to expand presidential authority. Danner cites more than 140 executive orders in Trump’s first hundred days and at least ten declared emergencies, including on trade, energy, and the border. The essay says this approach reframed ordinary policy disputes as emergencies requiring action by the president. Danner’s central criticism is that Congress, which is meant to check executive power, did not effectively resist. He attributes lawmakers’ silence to Trump’s influence over Republican voters, fear of primary challenges, and the political rewards of staying aligned with him. The phrase “constitutional dictatorship” is Danner’s interpretation of that combination of emergency declarations and weakened congressional oversight. The article is a political essay reviewing an inside account of the administration, not a judicial ruling or a formal finding that the constitutional order has ended.

title: Trump's Emoluments Clause Violations
description_medium: Donald Trump's use of his presidency to increase his personal wealth has raised concerns among legal and ethics experts. Trump has earned an 'unprecedented' $2.2 billion in income during his second term, and his crypto, airplane, and other business ventures have been accused of violating the emoluments clause. The clause prohibits federal officials from accepting gifts or payments from foreign governments.
description_long: A 2026 Slate legal Q&A revisits whether Trump’s crypto, airplane, and other business ventures could violate the Constitution’s emoluments clauses. It distinguishes the Foreign Emoluments Clause, which restricts federal officials from accepting presents or payments from foreign states without congressional consent, from the Domestic Emoluments Clause, which limits the president to a fixed salary and bars additional benefits from the federal government or states. The article presents a legal question about how those provisions apply to a president whose private businesses may receive payments while he holds office. Its discussion is commentary by legal writers, not a court judgment finding a violation. The issue turns on the source and nature of a benefit and whether it falls within the constitutional text. The legal analysis presents an open constitutional question rather than resolving how a court would apply the clauses to each venture.

title: Trump Promised a Sex-Trafficking Crackdown, But His Justice Department Hasn't Delivered
description_short: Trump Promised a Sex-Trafficking Crackdown, But His Justice Department Hasn't Delivered
description_medium: The Trump administration has called sex trafficking enforcement a priority, but a 2026 report found investigations had stalled and prosecutions declined over six months. Interviews with 25 former prosecutors, current agents, and victims’ advocates, along with federal court records, identified staffing shortages, funding cuts, immigration enforcement, and victims’ distrust of government as contributing factors.
description_long: The Trump administration has repeatedly described the fight against sex trafficking as a priority, but investigations stalled and prosecutions declined during the six months covered by a 2026 Japan Times report. The reporting drew on interviews with 25 former prosecutors, current agents, and victims’ advocates, as well as a review of federal court records. Those sources cited staffing shortages, funding cuts, immigration enforcement, and growing distrust of government among victims as reasons cases were not advancing. Former federal prosecutor Jacqueline Kelly, who led the prosecution of Sean Combs, said a stated priority cannot be delivered without adequate resources. The report describes a gap between the administration’s public emphasis and the capacity investigators and prosecutors said they had to pursue cases. Its account connects staffing and funding decisions with the willingness of victims to cooperate, making enforcement depend on both agency resources and trust. The stalled cases did not necessarily share one obstacle, but the report describes a broader decline observed by people working in the field.
